region: Indonesia — Bali and the Lesser Sunda Islands
description: Named for the island of Solor in Indonesia; terminal males develop a fiery red head over a violet-blue body and flare their fins at females during late-afternoon courtship. Like other fairy wrasses it spends the night wrapped in a mucus cocoon among rubble.

region: Western Pacific — mainly the Philippines
description: A Philippine fairy wrasse of rubble slopes; terminal males are orange-pink with deep red dorsal and pelvic fins that they raise like banners while displaying to their harem.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & eastern Indonesia
description: One of the smaller fairy wrasses, living in loose groups a few metres above rubble on outer reef slopes. Displaying males turn intense magenta with a yellow-orange back and flare their dark pelvic fins.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Tuamotus, north to southern Japan
description: The most widespread fairy wrasse, and its colours differ noticeably between Indian Ocean and Pacific populations. A dark spot on the upper caudal peduncle marks both sexes, and displaying males light up with electric-blue lines.

region: Western Pacific — southern Japan to Indonesia, east to Fiji & Tonga
description: One of the largest fairy wrasses, usually found on rubble slopes below about 20 m. Males are pink to lavender with yellow-centred dorsal, anal and caudal fins boldly edged in red.

region: Western & central Pacific — Great Barrier Reef to the Pitcairn Islands
description: Ranges further east than most fairy wrasses, from the Great Barrier Reef to Pitcairn. Terminal males are vividly red, purple and green and spend much of the day displaying to the females of their harem.

region: Hawaiian Islands (endemic)
description: Endemic to Hawaii, where it lives over rubble and sand patches on deeper reef slopes. Terminal males are flame-red above shading to yellow below, while females are paler and pinker.

region: Coral Sea — Great Barrier Reef & New Caledonia
description: A Coral Sea species of deeper rubble slopes, notable for the long, lance-shaped tail of the male. Males are golden-yellow with fine purple-blue lines running along the flank.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Andaman Sea to the Philippines & southern Japan
description: Lives in large mixed aggregations above reef slopes, picking zooplankton from the current. The name means "blue side", for the bright blue-edged scales on the forward flank of displaying males.

region: Coral Sea — New Caledonia & the Great Barrier Reef
description: Named for the French diver and photographer Pierre Laboute, it is known mainly from New Caledonia and the southern Great Barrier Reef. Males are rosy pink with bold magenta and yellow stripes along the flank.

region: Red Sea & western Indian Ocean to Sri Lanka
description: A small fairy wrasse that forms large, busy aggregations just above the reef, hence its common name. Males have greatly elongated red pelvic fins that trail beneath the body during display.

region: Micronesia — Caroline, Mariana & Marshall Islands
description: A Micronesian fairy wrasse whose name means "yellow-striped", for the golden band along the upper flank that stands out against the male's magenta-purple body.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines, Indonesia & Palau
description: A small fairy wrasse of rubble slopes; the male's bright yellow dorsal fin and yellow-washed back contrast sharply with its pink to red body.

region: Indonesia — Java, Bali & Sulawesi
description: Males carry long whip-like filaments on the dorsal fin, which they raise while racing around their females in display. The body shades from red-orange above to violet-blue below.

region: Western Pacific — Papua New Guinea & the Great Barrier Reef to Fiji & Tonga
description: Often found in shallower lagoon and back-reef rubble than its deep-water relatives. Both sexes are peppered with fine dark spots, and males develop violet tones and long pelvic fins.

region: Indonesia — northern Sulawesi & the Molucca Sea
description: Described in 1999 from northern Sulawesi; displaying males have a vivid orange back and dorsal fin over a magenta-purple lower body.

region: Western Pacific — southern Japan & Taiwan
description: A rarely exported fairy wrasse from deep reef slopes of southern Japan and Taiwan; males are distinguished by a long, lance-shaped tail and a pink body washed with yellow above.

region: Micronesia — Marshall Islands & Pohnpei
description: Known from deeper outer-reef slopes in the Marshall Islands and Pohnpei. Males are golden yellow with violet-edged fins and a diamond-shaped (rhomboid) tail.

region: Central Indian Ocean — Chagos Archipelago & Maldives
description: Described from the Chagos Archipelago and exported mainly from the Maldives. Its name ("red scales") refers to the patch of crimson scales on the male's lower forward flank.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines, Indonesia, Palau & southern Japan
description: Males hold harems over rubble and, especially in late afternoon, "flash" — racing above the females with every fin spread and colours briefly intensified. The tall red dorsal fin carries a few elongated rays.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Solomon Islands & Great Barrier Reef
description: Named for the many long filaments that trail from the male's dorsal fin and are raised during display flights over the harem. Forms mixed groups with other flashers and fairy wrasses over rubble.

region: Indian Ocean & western Pacific — East Africa to Indonesia
description: Unlike many flashers, the male has no long filaments; instead its tall, sail-like dorsal fin is red with an electric-blue border. Courting males flash over rubble patches in the late afternoon.

region: Red Sea (endemic)
description: A Red Sea endemic named for the eight blue-violet lines along its orange flanks. The male's dorsal fin is tall and rounded rather than filamentous.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia
description: Its blue flank lines are broken into rows of dots and dashes, which separates it from the similar Carpenter's flasher. Males display over rubble in late afternoon with all fins spread.

region: Indonesia — Sulawesi, Halmahera & Raja Ampat
description: Described in 1999 from Indonesia; when flashing, males turn an intense violet-blue below an orange-red back.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines
description: Males are told apart from other flashers by their bright yellow anal fin beneath an orange-red, blue-lined body. Like its relatives it lives in harems a metre or two above rubble.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia
description: Named for the angular outline of the male's dorsal fin. Displaying males show orange-red flanks with blue lines and a deep red dorsal fin.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: Darts constantly among rock crevices hunting tiny crustaceans, pest flatworms and pyramid snails, and sleeps in a mucus cocoon. Often turns into a persistent bully toward smaller, more peaceful fish.

region: Central & western Pacific — Micronesia to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: A secretive cousin of the sixline wrasse with four bright blue stripes on a bronze upper body above a violet belly. Notably aggressive toward other small wrasses.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: The largest Pseudocheilinus, recognised by eight thin dark lines on a pinkish body. An efficient hunter of pest snails and bristleworms that grows more aggressive with age.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii
description: Also called the disappearing wrasse: it lives deep in rubble and coral heads and is rarely seen in the open. Reddish with fine pale striations and a white streak below the eye.

region: Western & central Pacific — Philippines & Micronesia to Samoa
description: A deep-reef wrasse, usually below 20 m, with a violet forebody fading into a yellow rear and a black eyespot near the tail. Comparatively rarely collected and highly prized.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia
description: A tiny, secretive wrasse of sheltered inshore reefs, purple with pinkish streaks along the flank. It stays close to rock and coral cover and is one of the most peaceful wrasses for small reefs.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Marquesas & Pitcairn
description: Creeps through caves and crevices rather than swimming in the open, rarely leaving cover. Yellow-ringed black eyespots on the rear dorsal and anal fins, plus black pelvic fins, likely misdirect predators.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: A smaller, deeper-living relative of the sharpnose possum wrasse with narrow white rather than yellow bars. It lives deep within reef crevices and is seldom seen by divers.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Line Islands
description: Runs cleaning stations visited by hundreds of reef fish a day, advertising with a bobbing dance and removing parasites and dead tissue. Most wild-caught individuals fail to adapt to aquarium diets, so its collection is widely discouraged.

region: Hawaiian Islands (endemic)
description: Hawaii's endemic cleaner wrasse, more colourful than its widespread relative with a yellow head and a magenta-violet rear half. It services a wide range of reef fish at fixed cleaning stations.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Line Islands & Marquesas
description: Unlike the bluestreak cleaner it roams widely instead of holding a fixed station, cleaning fish across a large home range. Adults are dark in front and pale yellow behind, with a dark crescent in the tail.

region: Red Sea & Gulf of Aden
description: Juveniles are dedicated cleaners of other fish, but adults switch to feeding mainly on coral polyps. Its deep blue body bears two electric-blue lines along each side.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa
description: A thick-lipped wrasse that feeds on live coral polyps and mucus, while juveniles also clean other fish part-time. Adults have a golden-yellow back and a pale wedge in the tail.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii
description: A slender, fast-swimming wrasse that dives into the sand to sleep. Females are salmon-pink, while terminal males turn blue-green with a yellow-and-blue stripe along the lower flank.

region: Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Maldives & Sri Lanka to Indonesia
description: Named after underwater photographer Mike Severns. A slender sand-sleeping wrasse whose terminal males are greenish blue with fine lines, while females are orange-pink.

region: Pacific — Indonesia to the Line Islands & the eastern Pacific
description: A restless forager of shallow reef flats that is almost never still. Both sexes carry a bright red-orange mark above the pectoral fin — the "red shoulder".

region: Hawaiian Islands & Johnston Atoll
description: Endemic to Hawaii and Johnston Atoll, where it forages over shallow reef flats. Terminal males are green with a bright orange belt along the flank edged by blue lines.

region: Pacific — Cocos-Keeling & Christmas Islands to Hawaii & the Marquesas
description: Its long, tubular snout probes coral branches and crevices for small crustaceans and brittle stars. Males are deep blue-green, while females are pale in front shading to black behind with an orange upper snout.

region: Indian Ocean — Red Sea & East Africa to the Andaman Sea
description: The Indian Ocean counterpart of the Pacific bird wrasse, using its long beak to pick prey from coral crevices. Males are deep blue; females are paler with a dark rear and finely spotted flanks.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Christmas Island to the Marshall Islands, Japan to Australia
description: A bright yellow wrasse that dives into the sand at night or when frightened, and may stay buried for days after being moved. Prized in reef tanks for picking off flatworms and other small pests.

region: Indian Ocean — Maldives & Sri Lanka to western Indonesia
description: Named for its two-tone colouring — lemon-yellow above, white below — with black spots on the dorsal fin. Like other Halichoeres it buries itself in the sand to sleep.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Females and juveniles are white with bold black stripes and eyespots on the fins, while terminal males turn green with orange lines and a dark spot at the tail base. A useful hunter of flatworms and small pest snails; also called Hoeven's wrasse.

region: Hawaiian Islands & Johnston Atoll
description: Green with rows of red-pink scale markings and bold red bands on the head, a colour scheme that earned it the trade name "Christmas wrasse". Restricted to Hawaii (the look-alike elsewhere in the Pacific is Claudia's wrasse, H. claudia), it buries in sand at night and hunts small crustaceans by day.

region: Western Indian Ocean — East Africa, Madagascar & the Mascarenes
description: A western Indian Ocean wrasse whose adults combine an orange-brown body with a paler, pink-lined head and a white-ringed black eyespot on the dorsal fin. It sleeps buried in the sand.

region: Western Indian Ocean — East Africa & the Mascarenes to the Maldives
description: A small, peaceful sand-sleeper of the western Indian Ocean, green with pink stripes along the body and black eyespots on the dorsal fin.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Marquesas
description: Adults have a dark checkerboard of scale markings and a bright yellow spot below the dorsal fin; juveniles are black and white with the same yellow spot. A bold forager that turns over rubble for crustaceans and molluscs.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Green with bold red-pink lines and two white-ringed black eyespots on the dorsal fin — the "biocellatus" of its name. A peaceful, reef-safe sand-sleeper.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida through the Caribbean to Brazil
description: Terminal males have a yellow head, a black bar behind the pectoral fin and a blue-green rear; juveniles are bright yellow with a blue stripe. A common forager over Caribbean reefs.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida & the Caribbean to Brazil
description: A deeper-water Caribbean wrasse, yellow below with a broad navy-blue band along the back from head to tail. Large and robust, it hunts crabs and other invertebrates.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina & Bermuda to Brazil
description: Terminal males are greenish with a large dark blotch on the mid-flank and red-lined heads, while initial-phase fish are white with a black midlateral stripe and yellow back.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina & Bermuda to Brazil
description: The largest Halichoeres, reaching half a metre in the wild; adults are blue-green with gold mottling and a dark spot at the base of the pectoral fin. It feeds on snails, crabs and urchins, and is mostly seen in public aquaria.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina & Bermuda to Brazil, including the Gulf of Mexico
description: Common on shallow reefs, rubble and seagrass, and recognisable by two dark stripes along a pale greenish body. It dives into the sand when threatened and to sleep.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to New Caledonia
description: A wrasse of shallow lagoons and seagrass beds; adults are pale pastel green with faint darker markings, while juveniles are mottled green and brown for camouflage among the grass.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to Japan
description: Adults are dark blue-grey in front, shading abruptly to yellow over the rear half; juveniles are white with black stripes. It forages among coral and rubble on reef slopes.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Cocos-Keeling to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Picks tiny crustaceans and foraminiferans from rubble almost continuously, and needs a deep sand bed to sleep in. Females are cream with dense dark leopard spots; terminal males develop a green body with an orange, black-edged network.

region: Red Sea & western Indian Ocean — East Africa to the Maldives
description: Females have an orange upper body and a darker lower half densely covered in bright blue spots — the "divided" pattern of its name (sold as the blue star leopard wrasse). Terminal males are green-blue with orange vermiculations.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Indonesia to the Philippines & northern Australia
description: Covered in orange-red spots on a greenish body, with a dark, blue-ringed spot on the gill cover. A specialist micropredator that sifts copepods and tiny snails from rubble.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Darker than other leopard wrasses: females are near-black with pale greenish spots, while males show orange-brown markings. Named after the island of Negros in the Philippines.

region: Western Pacific — eastern Australia, mainly the Great Barrier Reef
description: A small leopard wrasse named after Australian reef-fish biologist Howard Choat; pale with large orange-red spots and a dark spot on the gill cover. Mostly exported from Queensland.

region: Hawaiian Islands & Johnston Atoll
description: A Hawaiian endemic covered in blue-edged dark spots on an orange-brown body, giving a glazed, pottery-like look. It forages over rubble and sand on shallow reefs.

region: Hawaiian Islands (endemic)
description: Endemic to Hawaii; females (sold as the redtail tamarin) are dark brown with a white spot on each scale and a red-tipped tail, while males develop a psychedelic orange-red head scrawled with blue.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: Females are black with a white spot on every scale and a bright yellow tail; terminal males look entirely different, orange-brown with a vertical blue line on each scale.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: Easily recognised by its yellow chest and the white-ringed black eyespots at the rear of the dorsal and anal fins. Unlike most tamarins, males and females look much alike.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Easter Island
description: Females are olive-brown with a blue dash on each scale; terminal males develop blue-lined heads and a pale vertical bar across the flank. One of the larger tamarins, growing well over 30 cm in the wild.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia to Samoa, north to Japan, south to eastern Australia
description: Black above and white below with small blue spots on the head; it forages over rubble and sand, where it also sleeps buried.

region: Subtropical south-western Pacific — eastern Australia & Lord Howe to New Caledonia & Easter Island
description: One of the few reef fish in which the female is the showier sex — hence the name: she is bright orange with electric-blue stripes, while the male is a more sombre blue-green.

region: Pacific — Christmas Island to Hawaii & the Tuamotus (replaced by C. cuvieri in the Indian Ocean)
description: Juveniles are bright orange with five black-edged white saddles; adults transform into a dark reddish-blue fish dotted with electric-blue spots and a vivid yellow tail. It flips rocks and rubble in search of crabs, snails and other invertebrates.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Line Islands
description: Juveniles are white with two large orange-rimmed eyespots on the dorsal fin, but adults turn dark green, develop a forehead hump and can exceed a metre. A powerful forager that overturns rocks for urchins, crabs and molluscs.

region: Indian Ocean — East Africa to Sri Lanka
description: Juveniles are orange-red with black-edged white saddles; adults turn dusky green with dark spots, blue-edged fins and green lines radiating from the eye. Also sold as the formosa wrasse.

region: Eastern Atlantic & Mediterranean — Gulf of Guinea to Norway
description: A common Mediterranean wrasse that buries in sand at night. Initial-phase fish are brownish with a pale stripe, while terminal males are blue-green with a zigzag orange band and a black blotch behind the pectoral fin.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Line Islands
description: A hardy, boisterous wrasse that patrols the reef constantly and grows more aggressive with age. Adults have a yellow crescent-moon centre to the tail and pink-banded green heads.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida through the Caribbean to Venezuela
description: Most individuals are yellow initial-phase fish; terminal males have a blue head separated from a green body by black-and-white bars. A classic case of sex change: if the territorial male disappears, the largest female becomes male within days.

region: Eastern Pacific — Gulf of California to Peru & the Galápagos
description: Initial-phase fish wear stripes of yellow, red and black; terminal males have a purple head, a yellow collar and a deep red body. Juveniles sometimes pick parasites from other fish.

region: Hawaiian Islands & Johnston Atoll
description: One of Hawaii's most common reef fish; adults have a blue head, an orange-red "saddle" behind the gills and a green body with fine vertical lines.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: Named for the six black saddles along its back that taper to points on the flank, with pink lines radiating from the eye. An active, aggressive swimmer of shallow lagoons and reef flats.

region: Red Sea (endemic)
description: The Red Sea's counterpart of the moon wrasse, green with pinkish-red vertical lines on each scale and pink bands on the head. Abundant on shallow Red Sea reefs.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Maldives to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: A bold black-and-yellow wrasse of shallow reef tops; broad dark saddles alternate with yellow-green bands along the body.

region: Eastern Atlantic & Mediterranean — Portugal & the Azores to the Gulf of Guinea
description: A warm-water Mediterranean wrasse, also called the ornate wrasse; females are green with a single dark bar across the body, while males have a red-and-blue banded head and a vivid blue bar behind the pectoral fin.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: Lives in the surge zone of exposed reef fronts, moving easily through breaking waves. Green with pink-red stripes along the flank and pink lines on the head.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: Initial-phase fish gather in small groups to feed on plankton above the reef; terminal males are vividly coloured with a green-blue head, a yellow collar and a purple body.

region: Indo-Pacific — Sri Lanka to Hawaii & the Marquesas, north to Japan and south to Lord Howe
description: Named for its yellow-to-green body and pink-banded head; it ranges widely into subtropical waters around Japan, Australia and the Kermadecs.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: Uses its thick, fleshy lips to take mouthfuls of sand and filter out small invertebrates. Adults are pale in front and dark behind, with green-and-pink lines on the head.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: Bold black-and-white bars and a green, pink-lined head identify this thick-lipped wrasse, which sifts sand and rubble for crustaceans, worms and molluscs.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: An elongate, fast-swimming predator of small fish and crustaceans over sand and rubble. Adults are pale blue-green with many thin orange-brown rings around the body; juveniles are white with three red stripes.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii & Easter Island
description: An extremely elongate wrasse of seagrass beds and weedy reef flats, where its green, brown or yellow colouring matches the vegetation. It stalks small crustaceans, snails and fish.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida through the Caribbean
description: A schooling, plankton-feeding wrasse that gathers in large purple shoals in mid-water along Caribbean reef drop-offs, often far above the bottom.

region: Eastern Pacific — northern California to Baja California
description: A cigar-shaped wrasse of Californian kelp forests that picks parasites off other fish, and buries itself in the sand at night.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil
description: Purple-blue over the upper front of the body and bright yellow elsewhere. Juveniles set up cleaning stations and pick parasites off larger reef fish.

region: Western Atlantic — South Carolina & Bermuda to Brazil
description: Bright red with a yellow upper rear and tail, a white stripe below the eye and a black spot at the tip of the pectoral fin. A deeper-water Caribbean species; its yellow juveniles clean other fish.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Christmas Island to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: The body is divided diagonally into a dark maroon forebody and a pale yellow-white rear; juveniles are black with bright yellow spots. Also sold as the coral hogfish.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Marquesas
description: Named for the black spot at the base of the pectoral fin (the "axil"); adults are red-brown in front and white behind, while juveniles are black with large white spots and often clean other fish.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: Reddish-brown with a row of pale spots along the back and black spots on the pelvic, anal and dorsal fins. Juveniles are dark with white spots and act as part-time cleaners.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Line Islands
description: A deeply forked, lyre-shaped tail edged in black sets it apart from other hogfish; the orange-brown forebody gives way to a white, dark-spotted rear.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to New Caledonia, north to southern Japan
description: Juveniles are yellow with a large black saddle beneath the rear of the dorsal fin; adults keep the saddle on a pinkish, finely lined body and can exceed half a metre. Also called the tarry hogfish.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Micronesia, north to southern Japan
description: A small, deep-water hogfish rarely over 10 cm, yellow-orange with thin red lines; one of the few Bodianus small enough for a modest reef aquarium.

region: Western Pacific — Taiwan & the Ryukyus to the Great Barrier Reef & New Caledonia
description: Named for its bright blue canine "tusks", used to crush crabs, snails and urchins. Blue-edged orange bars cross a white body; Australian fish are the most intensely coloured.

region: Western Atlantic — Nova Scotia & Bermuda through the Gulf of Mexico & Caribbean to northern South America
description: Roots through sand with its long, protrusible snout for clams, crabs and urchins; the first three dorsal spines form long streamers. A large, prized food fish often shown in public aquaria.

region: Eastern Pacific — Monterey Bay to the Gulf of California
description: A large kelp-forest wrasse whose powerful jaws crush sea urchins, helping keep kelp forests in balance. All start as reddish females; large males develop a black head and tail, a red midsection and a white chin.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Panama
description: True to its name, it flips over rocks and rubble to expose crabs, worms and urchins. Juveniles mimic drifting seaweed with long, flag-like dorsal rays and a swaying motion; it is also sold as the dragon wrasse.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Mexico
description: Dives headfirst into the sand to escape danger and travels short distances beneath the surface. Juveniles imitate drifting leaves, with the first two dorsal spines raised like a stalk.

region: Atlantic & Mediterranean — North Carolina to Brazil, and the Mediterranean & eastern Atlantic
description: A steep-headed, highly compressed wrasse of open sand that dives into the bottom at the slightest threat. Males defend large sandy territories containing several females.

region: Western Atlantic — Bahamas & Florida to the Lesser Antilles
description: Lives in loose colonies on open sand flats, each fish diving into the sand when threatened. Rosy pink with a pale belly and a steep, blunt forehead.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: A stealthy predator that often shadows other fish to snap up small fish and crustaceans they flush out. Named for the oblique lines across its cheeks.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Marquesas
description: A small, cryptic wrasse of rubble and seagrass, mottled red, green and brown with a dark spot mid-flank and another behind the eye. Males grow a long, pointed tail.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: Its jaws can shoot forward into a tube more than half the length of its head — one of the most extreme jaw protrusions known in fishes — to engulf shrimp and small fish. Colour varies from bright yellow to dark brown.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: One of the largest reef fish, growing to around 2 m with a pronounced forehead hump; it is among the few predators that eat crown-of-thorns starfish and toxic boxfish. Listed as Endangered and kept only in large public aquaria.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: Bold black-and-white bars with an orange-red head and breast; it forages over sand and rubble for crabs, molluscs and small fish, often following other foraging fish.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: Mottled olive-brown with white spots and tiny orange dots that camouflage it among rubble and seagrass, where it hunts crabs and snails.

region: Red Sea, Gulf of Aden & Persian Gulf
description: Males have a ragged, broom-like tail whose filaments trail behind them; the green body is set off by yellow pectoral fins and an orange-spotted head. A predator of crabs, snails and urchins on Red Sea reefs.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: A small, secretive wrasse that lurks among seaweed, soft corals and rubble, stalking tiny crustaceans. Mottled red-brown with pale head lines and a dark spot on the gill cover.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Japan & Australia
description: Males have the first dorsal spines drawn out into long streamers that are flicked during display; it lives among seagrass, weed and rubble.

region: Northeastern Atlantic & Mediterranean — Norway to Senegal
description: All begin life as orange-pink females with dark saddles near the tail; large individuals change sex into males with a vivid blue head and blue stripes on an orange body. Males build and guard nests in rock crevices.

region: Northeastern Atlantic — Norway to Morocco, including the British Isles
description: The largest European wrasse, mottled green-brown with pale spots; it is farmed and stocked as a "cleaner fish" to remove sea lice from salmon in net pens. Males build seaweed nests in crevices and can live more than 20 years.

region: Northwestern Atlantic — Nova Scotia to South Carolina
description: A stocky, blunt-headed wrasse of rocky shores, jetties and wrecks that crushes mussels and crabs with strong teeth. It becomes torpid in winter, sheltering in crevices until the water warms.

region: Northwestern Atlantic — Newfoundland to Chesapeake Bay
description: A small, hardy wrasse of New England docks, kelp and jetties that overwinters in a torpid state wedged into rock crevices.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean & western Pacific — Andaman Sea to Vanuatu, north to the Ryukyus
description: Terminal males are green with an orange-pink wash and blue-green markings around the mouth. Like other parrotfish it scrapes algae from dead coral with fused, beak-like teeth and sleeps in a mucus cocoon.

region: Red Sea, Gulf of Aden & Persian Gulf
description: Initial-phase fish are rust-brown with a yellow tail, while terminal males are green with pink-edged scales. One of the most common parrotfish on Red Sea reefs, where it produces large amounts of coral sand.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida through the Caribbean to Brazil
description: Terminal males are blue-green with orange-edged scales and orange bands around the mouth; initial-phase fish are dark grey with a broad white stripe. Each night it secretes a mucus cocoon before sleeping.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida through the Caribbean to Brazil
description: A common small Caribbean parrotfish; initial-phase fish are striped dark brown and white, while terminal males are blue-green with an orange-yellow band along the flank.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil
description: Initial-phase fish are white with three dark stripes and forage in roving groups over seagrass and reef; terminal males are blue-green with a pink-orange stripe.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Argentina
description: The largest herbivorous fish in the Atlantic, exceeding a metre; its juveniles depend on mangroves as nurseries, leaving the species vulnerable to mangrove loss. Adults have an orange-brown head and green, bronze-edged scales.

region: Western Atlantic — Maryland & Bermuda to Brazil
description: Bright blue at every size, with a squarish hump developing on the snout of large adults. It grazes algae on reefs and in nearby mangrove areas, often in roving groups.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — East Africa to Panama
description: Initial-phase fish are reddish-brown with dark speckles, like glowing embers; terminal males are green, usually darker in front than behind, with a steep, blunt head.

region: Red Sea (Indo-Pacific populations are now usually treated as C. ocellatus)
description: Juveniles are white with an orange band across the head and an orange-ringed black eyespot on the dorsal fin; adults turn green with pink-edged scales and a pink-and-green speckled head.

region: Red Sea & Indian Ocean (Pacific populations are now treated as C. spilurus)
description: Initial-phase fish are dark brown, often with a pale rear and a dark spot at the tail base; terminal males are green with an orange cheek. Studies on this species showed that its night-time mucus cocoon shields it from blood-feeding parasitic isopods.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Terminal males are green with a large pale cheek patch; initial-phase fish are dark brown crossed by several narrow pale bars.

region: Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Pitcairn Islands
description: Large adults develop a strikingly steep, almost vertical forehead profile. A powerful bioeroder that bites chunks from dead coral and grinds them into sand.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil
description: Initial-phase fish have a dark mottled back and a bright red belly; terminal males are green with a yellow spot at the top of the gill cover — the "stoplight" — and pink bands on the head. A major producer of sand on Caribbean reefs.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil
description: Named for the orange-red band running back from the corner of the mouth; terminal males are green with a small black-and-yellow spot above the pectoral fin.

region: Mediterranean & eastern Atlantic — Portugal & the Azores to Senegal
description: Unusually, the females are the colourful sex — red with a yellow saddle and a black blotch behind the head — while males are dull grey. The only parrotfish native to the Mediterranean.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Shares a burrow with an alpheid pistol shrimp, which digs while the goby stands guard and flicks its tail to warn of danger. Its tall, sail-like first dorsal fin bears a large black eyespot.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: One of the most widely kept shrimp gobies: pearly white with broad orange-red bars and small blue dots. It keeps watch at the burrow entrance while its pistol-shrimp partner maintains the tunnel.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Pale with scattered orange-yellow spots and faint brown saddles. It pairs with a pistol shrimp and perches at the burrow mouth, darting inside at the first sign of danger.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Solomon Islands
description: Broad dark-brown bars alternate with pale bands dotted with blue; also sold as the metallic shrimp goby. Like its relatives it shares a burrow with a pistol shrimp.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: Named after Israeli zoologist Heinz Steinitz; cream with five brown bars and yellow spots on the dorsal fins. It forms a lasting partnership with an alpheid shrimp in sandy rubble.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: White with five red-orange bands and small blue spots; pairs with a pistol shrimp in sand and rubble near coral reefs.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Palau, north to southern Japan
description: Distinguished by a large, flag-like tail marked with yellow and blue, and bold red bars across its white body. Also called Yano's shrimp goby, it lives with pistol shrimps on sandy reef slopes.

region: Indian Ocean — Seychelles & Maldives to the Andaman Sea
description: Pearly white with pink-red bars and a red streak running down from the eye; its tail is patterned with yellow and red. Exported mainly from the Maldives, it shares a burrow with a pistol shrimp.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Named for the slanting orange-brown bars that cross its pale body; it is usually seen perched at a burrow shared with a pistol shrimp.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Pale with four broad brown bands and orange spots on the head and fins. Like other Amblyeleotris it relies on a near-blind pistol shrimp to dig, while it acts as the lookout.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Seychelles to Indonesia & the Philippines
description: A small goby that hovers in pairs above the burrow it shares with the tiger pistol shrimp (Alpheus randalli). Its yellow head, diagonal dark bands and long, black, threadlike first dorsal spine make it unmistakable.

region: Western Pacific — southern Japan, Taiwan & the Philippines to Indonesia
description: White with bold orange-red diagonal bands and a tall, filament-tipped first dorsal fin; its name comes from its Japanese name, yasha-haze. Pairs hover over a burrow shared with a pistol shrimp.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: White with diagonal dark bands and a bright yellow snout; it lacks the long dorsal filament of the hi-fin red-banded goby. Pairs hover a few centimetres above their shrimp's burrow.

region: Western Indian Ocean — Seychelles & Maldives
description: White with broad blackish-brown saddles and bands, known mainly from the Seychelles and Maldives. Like its relatives it pairs with a pistol shrimp and hovers just above the burrow.

region: Western Pacific — Singapore & Indonesia to the Solomon Islands, north to Japan & south to Australia
description: One of the most popular marine gobies, perching motionless at its burrow entrance and partnering with pistol shrimps when available. It occurs in yellow and grey-brown colour forms, both dotted with blue spots.

region: Western Pacific — Singapore, Indonesia & the Philippines to New Caledonia
description: A sturdy shrimp goby of silty lagoons and sheltered coastal reefs, mottled green-brown with pink and blue spots. Less colourful than its relatives but extremely hardy; sold as the Singapore shrimp goby.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Palau and the Solomon Islands
description: Named for the Y-shaped dark bars along its pale flanks; it lives with pistol shrimps in sandy and silty lagoons.

region: Red Sea, Persian Gulf & western Indian Ocean
description: Pale tan to yellowish with blue spots and faint bars; a common pistol-shrimp partner on sandy and silty bottoms.

region: Red Sea & western Indian Ocean
description: Pale with about nine dark bars and scattered blue spots, and a dark spot on the first dorsal fin. Lives with a pistol shrimp in sand and rubble, often in shallow lagoons.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to Japan & south to the Great Barrier Reef
description: A small, pale shrimp goby with rows of brown blotches and gold-orange specks; it lives with pistol shrimps on sandy reef flats and lagoon floors.

region: Western & central Pacific — Indonesia to Samoa & the Society Islands
description: Named for Tangaroa, the Polynesian god of the sea; pale with orange-brown dashes and a tall first dorsal fin. It shares burrows with pistol shrimps on sandy slopes.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Marshall Islands, north to southern Japan
description: A tiny, dark goby with a white "cap" on top of its head, which hovers above its pistol shrimp's burrow while constantly fanning its large pectoral fins.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Males have a very large mouth and a tall, flag-like first dorsal fin with a dark eyespot, which they raise in display. It lives with pistol shrimps on silty sand and mud bottoms.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Palau, north to southern Japan
description: Its tall, sail-like first dorsal fin is spotted and edged with yellow; pale with brown saddles, it partners with pistol shrimps on sandy and silty slopes.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Tuamotus, north to southern Japan
description: Constantly takes mouthfuls of sand and sieves out small invertebrates through its gills, keeping the sand bed stirred. Pairs dig burrows under rocks; its golden head carries an electric-blue cheek stripe.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: White with rows of orange spots and orange lines on the head; like other sleeper gobies it sifts sand constantly and lives in pairs in a burrow under rocks. Also called the maiden goby.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Named for the small, dark-edged blue spots on its cheek; pale with a black-tipped first dorsal fin. A common sand-sifting sleeper goby that lives in pairs.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: White with two black stripes along the body and a black spot on the first dorsal fin. Pairs dig burrows beneath rocks and can shift large amounts of sand.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Pale with broad brown-orange bars edged in blue and a dark eyespot on the first dorsal fin; usually found in pairs on silty sand near reefs.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Pale with a greenish-yellow band along the flank and small orange spots; pairs sift sand over silty lagoon bottoms.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Pale with a row of brown rectangular blotches and red-orange dots, and a pointed tail. Pairs build burrows under rocks and spend the day sifting sand.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to Japan & south to Australia
description: A sand-sifting goby that also grazes filamentous algae, often digging a burrow under rubble. Olive-green with five dark bars, blue-edged head stripes and a dark spot on the first dorsal fin.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Papua New Guinea
description: Pale with a crosshatched pattern of orange-brown lines; it lives on silty sand near reefs, where it digs a small burrow and sifts the sand for food.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: A larger relative of the banded goby, olive-brown with several dark bars, white speckles and blue lines below the eye; it builds burrows in silty sand and grazes algae and detritus.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Vanuatu, north to Palau & south to the Great Barrier Reef
description: Pairs move in jerky hops with both dorsal fins raised; the two large eyespots and spread fins are thought to mimic a crab and deter predators. A constant sand sifter of sheltered lagoons.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Micronesia, south to the Great Barrier Reef
description: Picks at film algae, diatoms and tiny invertebrates on rock and is hard to keep fed in tanks without abundant natural growth. Pale greenish with blue-edged orange stripes and a white-ringed eyespot on the second dorsal fin; also called the court jester goby.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Micronesia, north to southern Japan
description: Black with thin yellow lines from snout to tail and a yellow-ringed eyespot on the second dorsal fin. Like Rainford's goby it grazes biofilm and tiny invertebrates from rock.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Great Barrier Reef, north to the Ryukyus
description: A tiny, all-yellow goby that perches among the branches of Acropora and other corals, often in small groups. Like other clown gobies it lacks scales and protects itself with a bitter, toxic skin mucus.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Bright yellow with thin electric-blue lines across the head and along the bases of the fins. Pairs live in table and branching corals and lay their eggs on a patch of coral they clear themselves.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: Emerald green with thin red-pink bars on the head and fine red spots; pairs live among Acropora branches, where they lay eggs on a cleared patch of coral. Also called the broad-barred goby.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: A dull olive-brown clown goby with faint red-brown bars on the head; it shelters deep among the branches of Acropora colonies and rarely ventures out.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Near-black with five thin blue lines across the head; a coral-dwelling clown goby that rarely leaves the shelter of its host colony.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii
description: Spends its entire adult life on a single wire coral (Cirrhipathes), where a pair clears a band of tissue on which to lay eggs. Translucent with brown-orange bands that match the coral's polyps.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii
description: The largest Bryaninops, translucent with an orange-yellow internal glow; it lives on whip gorgonians and wire corals, picking plankton from the passing current.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Society Islands, north to southern Japan
description: One of the smallest reef fishes, a translucent goby with a yellow belly and brilliant pink-red eyes that hovers in small groups just above Acropora branches.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Marquesas
description: A tiny, cryptic goby that creeps over rubble flicking enormous banded pectoral fins and a spiky first dorsal fin. Often sold as the flaming prawn goby, it spends most of its time hidden in crevices.

region: Western Pacific — southern Japan & Taiwan to Indonesia & the Great Barrier Reef
description: A tiny orange goby covered in yellow and pink spots that hovers in loose groups beneath ledges and at cave mouths. A bidirectional sex changer: individuals can switch from female to male and back again depending on social rank.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Solomon Islands, north to southern Japan
description: Hovers in loose groups along steep reef walls and beneath overhangs, often oriented head-up; pale with a bluish sheen and an orange-yellow band along the back.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Solomon Islands & the Great Barrier Reef
description: A minute, translucent goby with two dark stripes along the body that lives in groups among the branches of hard corals. Like most dwarfgobies of its genus it lives fast, maturing within a few months.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: A secretive goby of caves and crevices, tan to orange with thin, dark-edged pale bars encircling the body. It is rarely seen far from cover.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida & Bermuda through the Caribbean
description: A rust-orange Caribbean goby that lives in reef caves, often resting upside-down on the ceiling or sideways on walls with its belly pressed to the rock.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: A sand-dwelling goby of lagoons and reef flats, pale with rows of brown spots and pearly blue flecks; it hops over sand and rubble, sifting mouthfuls for small invertebrates.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Common on shallow sand and mangrove-fringed flats, pale with a row of dark spots along the flank and pearly flecks; it tolerates silty, turbid water better than most reef gobies.

region: Indo-Pacific — Maldives to the Marshall Islands, north to southern Japan
description: Pale with dark midlateral spots and thin yellow-orange lines; it lives on sand and rubble near the reef base, perching between short hops.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: A translucent sand goby with orange flecks and a dark spot at the tail base; it rests on sand patches near reefs and darts off in short hops.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Translucent with orange-red spots and a black tip on the first dorsal fin, which it flicks as a signal; it rests on sand at the base of reefs.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida, the Bahamas & the Gulf of Mexico to Belize
description: Operates cleaning stations on coral heads, where larger fish — even groupers and moray eels — pose to have parasites removed. Widely captive-bred, it is one of the few marine fish that spawns readily in home aquaria.

region: Western Atlantic — Bahamas & the Caribbean
description: Its bright stripe may be yellow, white or blue depending on locality, meeting in a V on the snout. Like the neon goby it runs cleaning stations on coral heads.

region: Southwestern Atlantic — Brazil (endemic)
description: A Brazilian endemic cleaner goby, black with a bright yellow stripe from snout to tail. Heavy collection led to its protection in Brazil, and most in the trade are now captive-bred.

region: Eastern Pacific — Gulf of California to Ecuador & the Galápagos
description: An eastern Pacific cleaner goby with a bright red-orange head and a pale, dark-striped body; besides cleaning it picks small crustaceans from rock.

region: Western Atlantic — Caribbean coast of Colombia & Venezuela to the Lesser Antilles
description: Dark with a yellow stripe from snout to tail and a bright yellow nose; a Caribbean cleaner that perches on coral heads in pairs or small groups.

region: Western Atlantic — Bahamas & Cayman Islands to the western Caribbean
description: A Caribbean cleaner goby with a pale stripe along the dark body and a yellow V on the snout; it sets up cleaning stations on brain and star corals.

region: Eastern Pacific — central California to the Gulf of California
description: A brilliant red goby with electric-blue bars from the rocky reefs of southern California; it needs cool water and rarely lives more than two years. Like some Trimma, it can change sex in either direction.

region: Eastern Pacific — central California to Baja California & Guadalupe Island
description: A cool-water Californian goby with many narrow blue bars on a red body; it lives among rocks and cobble from the low intertidal to moderate depths.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida through the Caribbean
description: Hovers in loose aggregations beneath ledges and in caves, nearly transparent with a dark "mask" through the eye.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina & Bermuda to Brazil
description: A pale, nearly translucent sand goby with dark markings and a dark "bridle" line behind the eye; it rests on sand patches near reefs and darts away in short bursts.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida & the Bahamas through the Caribbean
description: A tiny goby that perches on living coral heads rather than sand; translucent yellow-orange with electric-blue markings on the head.

region: Western Atlantic — New York to Florida & the Gulf of Mexico
description: A scaleless goby of oyster reefs, estuaries and tidal creeks along the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts; males guard eggs laid on the inside of empty oyster shells.

region: Indo-Pacific — Mauritius & the Maldives to Samoa, north to the Ryukyus & south to New Caledonia
description: A deeper-living relative of the firefish, usually found below about 25 m, with a violet-washed head and a purple rear half. It hovers above its burrow picking plankton and darts headfirst inside when alarmed.

region: Western & central Pacific — Micronesia to the Tuamotus & Pitcairn
description: A prized dartfish of deep outer-reef slopes, typically below 25 m, whose golden-yellow head blends into a lavender-pink body. Like its relatives it hovers near a burrow and retreats tail-first or headfirst at any threat.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Society Islands
description: Adults swim in pairs a metre or so above the reef and dash into a burrow when threatened, while juveniles form small groups. The front half is pale blue-grey and the rear darkens to near-black; also called the scissortail dartfish.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Line Islands
description: Lives in colonies above shallow reef flats, hovering together and sharing burrows; its pale blue-green body is crossed by many thin pinkish bars edged in blue. Also sold as the Chinese zebra goby.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii
description: Pale powder-blue to yellowish with a black spot in the centre of the tail; it hovers in pairs or small groups over sand and rubble near its burrow.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Tuamotus, north to southern Japan
description: A pale, pearly blue-green dartfish of shallow lagoon sand flats, also called the blue gudgeon, usually seen in pairs or small groups that retreat into burrows when disturbed.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to New Caledonia, north to southern Japan
description: Pale blue with long, trailing filaments extending from the tail fin; it hovers over open sand near its burrow. Traded as the blue hana goby.

region: Indo-Pacific — Mauritius to Hawaii & the Society Islands
description: An elongate, worm-like fish that hovers just above the sand with an undulating body, diving into its burrow when disturbed. White with a yellow-orange stripe and a black spot at the base of the tail.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines, Indonesia & the Solomon Islands
description: Juveniles stream out of the burrow by day in dense schools, striped black and white like venomous catfish; adults stay underground excavating tunnel systems beneath rocks. Neither a goby nor a blenny, it is one of only two species in its own family.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Great Barrier Reef, north to southern Japan
description: A tiny triplefin (often listed as H. striatum) with three separate dorsal fins and neat orange, white and blue stripes; it perches on rocks and sponges and darts between perches.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Grazes filamentous algae from rock almost nonstop with comb-like teeth on mobile lips, hence its common name. Mottled olive and brown for camouflage, with branched cirri above the eyes; also called the jewelled rockskipper.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Papua New Guinea & Palau
description: Dark grey-brown peppered with tiny white "stars", with a tall forehead and branched cirri above the eyes. Like the lawnmower blenny it grazes algae from rock and sits perched on its pectoral fins.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: An all-dark blenny with a tall, sail-like dorsal fin that grazes algae among branching corals; juveniles of some Pacific populations are bright yellow.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Pale with dark bars and covered in orange-red spots on the head and forebody; it lives in the surge zone of reef crests, grazing algae from wave-washed rock.

region: Indo-Pacific — Maldives to the Phoenix Islands, north to southern Japan
description: Dark brown in front and bright orange behind, it peers out of an old worm hole or crevice and darts out to graze algae. Males guarding eggs turn red with white bars.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Marquesas
description: Unusually for a blenny, it swims up into open water to feed on plankton among schools of sea goldies, whose golden colour it mimics. Its lyre-shaped tail and habit of peering from holes make it a favourite.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Papua New Guinea
description: Small and peaceful, grey-brown in front fading to yellow behind, with a dark spot at the base of the tail. It grazes film algae and spends much of its time perched in holes.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Sri Lanka to Indonesia & the Philippines, north to southern Japan
description: Pale with dark stripes along the body that may break up into rows of spots; a peaceful grazer of film algae that perches in holes and on coral.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Solomon Islands, north to southern Japan
description: A large, dark combtooth blenny that holds a small territory on coral heads, grazing algae and keeping watch from a hole. Also called Namiye's blenny.

region: Red Sea & Gulf of Aden
description: A harmless combtooth blenny that mimics the venomous blackline fangblenny, copying its blue head, yellow rear and black stripe so that predators leave it alone.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Andaman Sea to Fiji, north to southern Japan
description: Pale grey with rows of dark spots and a white belly; a widespread small combtooth blenny of shallow reefs that perches on rock and coral.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Dark brown with red streaks and spots radiating over the head and a fringe of cirri across the nape; it perches in surge-swept crevices on shallow reefs, grazing algae.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: Males are dark with red-orange lines on the head, while females are chestnut-brown with a darker net pattern; it lives on reef flats and grazes algae.

region: Pacific — Micronesia to the Hawaiian & Pitcairn Islands
description: Dark brown with tiny red speckles and a fringe of cirri across the nape; common on surge-swept reef fronts throughout the Pacific islands.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii & the Society Islands
description: Feeds almost entirely on the polyps of Acropora and Pocillopora corals, living among their branches. Its pale body is covered in clusters of dark spots, which are reddish in males; males guard eggs laid on coral.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to the Great Barrier Reef, north to southern Japan
description: Carries a pair of large grooved fangs in the lower jaw linked to venom glands, so predators that grab it quickly spit it out. Several harmless blennies mimic its black-striped, yellow-tailed pattern.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: Blue-grey in front and bright yellow behind, with a black line running up from the eye onto the dorsal fin. Its venomous bite makes it a model for harmless mimics such as the bicolor fangblenny.

region: Eastern Indian Ocean — Sri Lanka & the Andaman Sea to Sumatra
description: Pale blue-grey with a black diagonal stripe from the eye to the dorsal fin, which is black with an electric-blue border; also called Smith's fangblenny. Like other fangblennies it hovers openly, protected by its venom.

region: Red Sea & Gulf of Aden
description: A venomous Red Sea fangblenny with a blue-grey head, a yellow rear and a black stripe along the upper flank; it is the model copied by the harmless Red Sea mimic blenny.

region: Western Pacific — Fiji
description: Coloured entirely canary-yellow, it hovers above the reef picking plankton, relying on its venomous fangs for protection.

region: Western Indian Ocean — East Africa, Madagascar & the Comoros
description: A western Indian Ocean fangblenny, grey-blue in front shading to yellow behind; like its relatives it swims openly above the reef, protected by a venomous bite.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Line Islands
description: Juveniles mimic the bluestreak cleaner wrasse, then dart out to bite scales, skin and mucus from passing fish. It shelters tail-first in old worm tubes.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Marquesas
description: Named for the "piano keys" of dark blocks along its pale flank; it ambushes passing fish from a hole to bite off scales and mucus.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Samoa, north to southern Japan
description: A non-venomous mimic of the forktail fangblenny whose borrowed blue-and-yellow colours let it approach other fish and nip their fins and scales.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Marquesas & Pitcairn
description: An uncanny mimic of the bluestreak cleaner wrasse that approaches fish expecting to be cleaned and tears off pieces of fin or skin instead. Its underslung mouth gives it away.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to New Caledonia, north to southern Japan
description: A harmless sabretooth blenny that mimics the venomous striped fangblenny; it lives among seagrass and rubble and lays its eggs inside empty shells or tubes.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: A small, mottled green blenny with a tall dorsal fin and branched cirri, camouflaged among seaweed and seagrass where it picks off small invertebrates and algae.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida through the Caribbean
description: A pugnacious algae-grazing blenny that defends its patch of rock against fish many times its size. Dark brown with bright red lips and red-edged fins.

region: Northeastern Atlantic & Mediterranean — Ireland & the North Sea to Morocco
description: A large, characterful blenny of rocky coasts with big branched tentacles over its eyes and dark saddles on a brown body; males guard eggs in crevices.

region: Western Atlantic — New York & Bermuda to Venezuela
description: A small, variably coloured blenny that perches among seaweed and rubble, ranging from mottled brown to bright yellow with a dark mark at the front of the dorsal fin.

region: Western Atlantic — Caribbean coasts of Colombia & Venezuela
description: Lives inside empty barnacle shells on pilings and rocks, peering out with large eyes; its blue-grey body is covered in orange-gold spots. Named after INVEMAR, the Colombian marine research institute.

region: Western Atlantic — Nova Scotia to Florida & the Gulf of Mexico
description: Named for the feathery cirri above its eyes; it lives among oyster reefs and shell beds in bays and estuaries along the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts.

region: Atlantic — tropical & warm-temperate shores on both sides, including the Mediterranean
description: A rugged algae-grazing blenny of tide pools and jetties on both sides of the Atlantic, with a crest of cirri running along the top of its head.

region: Northeastern Atlantic — Norway to Morocco, Madeira & the Azores
description: The common rock-pool blenny of European shores; at low tide it can survive for hours out of water under damp rocks and seaweed.

region: Western Atlantic — Bahamas & the Caribbean
description: Lives in an abandoned worm or barnacle hole in living coral, with only its spiny, cirri-crowned head showing as it snaps plankton from the passing current.

region: Western Atlantic — Bahamas & the Caribbean
description: A tiny tube blenny with a cluster of spines on top of its head; it occupies empty worm holes high on living coral heads and darts out after plankton.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida & the Bahamas through the Caribbean
description: Named for the rough, spiny crown on its head; it lives in vacated holes in coral, and males defend their hole by flaring their fins at intruders.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida & the Gulf of Mexico through the Caribbean
description: Males live in vacated worm holes and repeatedly pop out to flash a huge, sail-like dorsal fin, courting females and warning rivals.

region: Eastern Pacific — Gulf of California
description: The Gulf of California counterpart of the sailfin blenny; males signal from the mouth of their hole by repeatedly raising a tall, dark dorsal fin.

region: Western Atlantic — Bahamas & the Caribbean
description: A slender, translucent orange blenny that hovers near reef walls with its tail curled to one side, then straightens it to lunge at tiny fish and shrimp — an unusual predatory lifestyle for a blenny.
